design_detail: Record-review comparison of two counts of heroin-related deaths for deaths occurring in Victoria, Australia, from 1 January 2012 to 31 December 2013. Reference count (the authors' 'gold standard'): closed coronial cases in the National Coronial Information System (NCIS) returned by a broad search (heroin in the certified cause of death, parts 1a, 1b, 1c, 2 or 3; heroin in the NCIS field for the object (primary or secondary) that caused death, alone, with other drugs or as a keyword; heroin as a keyword in police, pathology and coronial reports; heroin, heroin and morphine, or morphine alone in toxicology reports; 9,060 records), each judged with the authors' previously published attribution model (Stam et al., 2017, ref 30), which weighs toxicological evidence (6-acetylmorphine, the morphine-to-codeine ratio, or morphine alone) and investigative evidence (circumstances, scene, clinical and pathological findings). Comparison count: deaths registered in Victoria in the national mortality data of the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW) to which Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) mortality coders assigned the heroin code T40.1 as an associated cause, with underlying cause X42, X44, X62, X64, X85, Y12 or Y14 (and F11 or F19 for deaths before 2013). The ABS codes held in the NCIS for each reference case were then used to classify missed cases by underlying-cause code (Table 1) and by how the coroner's finding attributed the death (Table 2). Counts and percentages only; no statistical tests.
can_establish: How many deaths in Victoria in 2012–2013 that met the authors' heroin-attribution model in closed coronial records did not carry the heroin code T40.1 in national mortality data, and at which steps they were lost: the coroner's wording, attribution to morphine or to generic drug toxicity, coding, and deaths never coded at all.
cannot_establish: That all 243 reference deaths were caused by heroin (the reference is the authors' own model, not validated here; 63 of the 243 had no 6-acetylmorphine detected; who applied the model, and whether blind to the codes, is not reported); how often national data wrongly add heroin deaths (only 4 such deaths, among records the search returned, were identified); whether the shortfall holds after 2013, when the ABS revision process changed, or outside Victoria; or why the 20 uncoded deaths were never coded (inferred by elimination).

sample.recruitment: Records: closed NCIS coronial cases for deaths in Victoria in 2012–2013, which typically held an autopsy and toxicology report, a police narrative and the coronial finding; national mortality data held by the AIHW, coded by the ABS (PDF pp. 5–7).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Reference: records returned by the four search strategies (9,060), duplicates removed, kept when the model judged the toxicological and investigative evidence sufficient to attribute the death to heroin; heroin overdose deaths and deaths from misadventure or impairment secondary to acute heroin intoxication were included; deaths in which heroin use was judged coincidental were excluded. Comparison: open and closed cases, registered in Victoria (not by residence), dated by date of death, with the codes listed above (PDF pp. 5–7, 9–10).
sample.demographics: Not reported: no age, sex or other characteristics of the 243 deaths, and no breakdown by year.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (records). How many of the 9,060 records failed which criterion is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: One state over two years, chosen so that coronial investigations would be finalized. The reference search covered closed NCIS cases only, while the comparison count included open and closed cases; heroin deaths still open at the search would be missing from the reference (how many cases were open is not stated). The reference includes 8 misadventure deaths from heroin intoxication, while the national comparison count required a drug-poisoning (or, before 2013, F11 or F19) underlying cause; 20 reference deaths had another underlying cause and so could not enter the national count as defined (key finding 13). The model was built by the same team (ref 30). One co-author is at the ABS Mortality Data Centre, whose coding is evaluated, and two at the Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine (PDF p. 1).

exposure.measurement: How a death entered each count, and who decided. Reportable deaths (unexpected, accidental, suspicious or of unknown cause) go to the coroner for medico-legal investigation (police, toxicology and pathology reports) and are first registered with the state Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, which passes them to the ABS; after the coroner's formal finding the certified cause of death reaches the NCIS; ABS mortality coders assign ICD-10 codes from both sources and the ABS supplies the AIHW (PDF p. 4; Figure 1, PDF p. 21). Reference count: the authors applied their model to NCIS records (PDF pp. 5–6); how many reviewers, whether they were blind to the ABS codes held in the NCIS, and their agreement are not reported. 'Attributed to heroin' meant heroin named, alone or with other drugs, in the certified cause of death or in the NCIS object-that-caused-death field (PDF p. 8). What was tested: NCIS cases typically held an autopsy and toxicology report (PDF p. 6); the share of the 243 with toxicology is not reported; 6-acetylmorphine was detected in 180 (74%, editors' calculation).
exposure.polysubstance: Not separated. The model attributes deaths to heroin alone or in combination with other drugs; 11 deaths were attributed to both heroin and morphine; the drugs found with heroin are not reported. Deaths certified as mixed or combined drug toxicity, with heroin listed only in the NCIS object field, were among those the coding missed (PDF pp. 11–12).

comparison.controls: The same deaths counted two ways: the reference count (NCIS records judged with the authors' model) against the national coded count (T40.1 assigned by ABS coders, reported by the AIHW). All 165 AIHW deaths were among the NCIS search results; 161 were among the 243 and 4 were excluded by the model. Neither count was checked against an independent standard.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (counts of deaths). Reasons heroin may go unidentified (rapid conversion to 6-acetylmorphine and then morphine; a long interval between use and death, including resuscitation and hospital admission; post-mortem redistribution and instability of 6-acetylmorphine, also in frozen samples) are described from the literature, not measured (PDF p. 5).

outcomes.instruments: Counts by ICD-10 underlying-cause code, AIHW against reference (Table 1, PDF p. 19); counts by attribution group with the number coded T40.1 (Table 2, PDF p. 20); time from death to case closure for the 20 uncoded deaths (PDF p. 10); a published national report for the same period (PDF p. 9).
outcomes.validity_norms: The attribution model is cited (ref 30) and not re-validated here; its strength-of-evidence categories are not reported for the 243 deaths.
outcomes.operationalization: Reference 'heroin-related death': judged by the model on toxicological and investigative evidence, including deaths with morphine alone in toxicology. 'Identified by the ABS': T40.1 as an associated cause. 'Missed': a reference death without T40.1.

analysis.effect_sizes: Reference 243 against AIHW 165: 78 fewer in the national data, that is 32.1% of 243 (the paper's 'underreported by 32%') and 47.3% of 165 (the paper's '47% greater'; editors' calculation). 161 of 243 reference deaths (66%) had T40.1; 82 (34%) did not; 4 T40.1 deaths were excluded by the model. By attribution group, coded T40.1: heroin toxicity 146 of 180 (81%); heroin and morphine 8 of 11 (73%); morphine or another opioid 5 of 39 (13%); generic drug toxicity 0 of 5; misadventure 2 of 8 (25%). Of 191 deaths the coroner attributed to heroin, 154 (81%) were coded T40.1 and 37 were not (3 of these coded T40.2 only). Of 44 drug-toxicity deaths not attributed to heroin, 5 (11%) were coded T40.1. By underlying cause, AIHW against reference: X44 69 against 98 (the largest difference), X42 75 against 79, Y14 10 against 12, Y12 4 against 5, F11 1 against 3, X64 6 against 6; 20 reference deaths had another underlying code and 20 none. Editors' calculation: taking the coroner's own attribution as the reference, coding missed 37 of 191 heroin-attributed deaths (19%).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; approved by the Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine Research Advisory Committee (RAC 030/14) and the Department of Justice and Regulation Human Research Ethics Committee (CF/15/2853) (PDF p. 8).
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract's shares of missed deaths (40%, 30%, 24%) cannot be reproduced from the tables; the 20 uncoded deaths are not broken down by attribution group; the model's evidence categories, the deaths' demographics and the national-data extraction date are not reported.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In Victoria in 2012–2013, 243 deaths met the authors' heroin-attribution model in closed coronial records, against 165 deaths with the heroin code T40.1 in national mortality data (161 of them among the 243; 4 judged coincidental by the model). Of the 82 reference deaths without T40.1, 37 had heroin named by the coroner, mostly in wording the coding did not pick up (3 were coded T40.2 only); 39 were certified as morphine, another opioid or generic drug toxicity; 6 were misadventure deaths; and 20 deaths, cutting across these groups, had no ICD-10 code at all.
interpretation_gap.claimed: (1) The abstract and Conclusion say heroin deaths were "underreported by 32%" and the Discussion that the actual number was 47% greater than 165 (PDF pp. 2, 13, 15); both treat the authors' unvalidated model as the true count, although 63 of its 243 deaths had no 6-acetylmorphine detected and who applied it is not reported. (2) The abstract gives late registration as the cause of 24% of missed deaths; the Results present it as the most reasonable explanation once closure time was excluded, without registration dates or closure times for coded deaths (PDF p. 10). (3) The abstract's 40% and 30% shares cannot be reproduced from the tables (reporting issue 1). (4) The Discussion asserts over-reporting of morphine-related deaths (PDF pp. 13–14), but no count of national morphine deaths is given; what is shown is that 34 deaths certified as morphine or another opioid were judged heroin-related by the model and lacked T40.1. (5) The Discussion says variability in a secondary report was demonstrated, from one national figure (220 deaths) whose derivation is not examined. The overcounting direction is measured only as the 4 coded deaths the model excluded.

timeline.event: Mertz, Janssen and Williams (Journal of Forensic Sciences, ref 24): a re-examination of unintentional overdose deaths in Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, found heroin-related deaths attributed to morphine and codeine toxicity and deaths missed through inconsistent certification, as Stam et al. describe it (PDF p. 13); not read for this card.
Stam, Gerostamoulos, Dietze et al. (Forensic Science International, ref 30): the attribution model used here as the reference count; not read for this card.
Ruhm (Addiction, ref 36): cited here for underreporting of opioid-related deaths through incomplete death certification to an extent similar to this study (PDF p. 14).

Horon et al. (Maryland, 2012–2015; card sc_horon_2018): certificates named heroin in 1,130 overdose deaths while 2,182 met an enhanced-surveillance protocol of certificate wording, toxicology markers and scene evidence; most of the additional deaths had morphine certified as the cause.
Darke's commentary (doi 10.1111/add.14520) and Robertson's letter (doi 10.1111/add.14627) on this paper, linked in PubMed; not among the files read for this card.

replication.where_it_stands: In Victoria, as in Maryland (card sc_horon_2018) and, as described here, Allegheny County, deaths certified as morphine or in generic multi-drug terms are the main source of shortfall in heroin-specific counts, and here also the wording of the coroner's finding (heroin only in the NCIS object field) and deaths never coded. None of these studies checks its reference count against an independent standard, and the overcounting direction is measured here only as 4 deaths. The commentary and letter published with this paper have not been read.

funding.funder: NCS (the first author) was supported by an Australian Government Research Training Program Scholarship; the research received no other specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors (PDF p. 15).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed in the accepted manuscript: no other authors declare any actual or potential conflict of interest (PDF p. 2). No declaration for any author precedes this sentence (reporting issue 6).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors at Monash University (Department of Forensic Medicine; Department of Community Emergency Health and Paramedic Practice; Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine), the Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine, Ambulance Victoria, and the Mortality Data Centre of the Australian Bureau of Statistics (Moran), whose coding is evaluated (PDF p. 1). The reference model is the team's own (ref 30). Recorded as flags for closer reading.

what_would_settle_it: Blinded review of a random sample of Victorian coronial cases, both those coded T40.1 and those the model calls heroin-related without it, by forensic pathologists outside the team using written criteria and reporting their agreement, followed by a repeat comparison of coronial records with final ABS data for deaths after the change in the ABS revision process.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: The NCIS holds the coronial records of reportable deaths, the right frame for heroin deaths; only closed cases were searched, while the national count included open cases.
All records returned by four broad search strategies (9,060) were assessed; no sampling.
243 reference deaths; some groups are small (5 generic, 8 misadventure, 11 heroin and morphine).

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: The reporting, coding and revision process is described with a diagram; no age, sex or year breakdown of the deaths is given.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All 243 deaths appear in both tables; the 20 uncoded deaths are not assigned to attribution groups.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: The reference combines a specific marker (6-acetylmorphine) with weaker ones (morphine-to-codeine ratio, morphine alone) and investigative evidence in a published model, but the model is the authors' own and not validated here; 63 of 243 had no 6-acetylmorphine.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Who applied the model, how many reviewers, whether they were blind to the ABS codes held in the NCIS, and their agreement are not reported.
Counts and percentages agree with the tables, but the abstract's 40% and 30% shares cannot be reproduced, and no uncertainty is given for the shortfall.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence fits a count of deaths compared under two definitions (round brief, certificate studies). The comparison is in effect a check of the national heroin code's sensitivity against the authors' own attribution model, which is reasonable (toxicology plus investigative evidence from full coronial files) but unvalidated and applied by unnamed reviewers who could see the codes. The counts are internally consistent; the abstract's breakdown of missed deaths is not. Citable for: in Victoria in 2012–2013, the national heroin code T40.1 was missing from 82 of 243 deaths that met the authors' model in coronial records, and the national count (165) was 78 lower; 37 of 191 deaths the coroner attributed to heroin were not coded as heroin, mostly because of how the cause was worded; most deaths certified as morphine, another opioid or generic drug toxicity were not coded as heroin; 20 deaths had no code at all. Not citable for: heroin as the cause of all 243 deaths, the accuracy of the national count in later years or other states, or the 40% and 30% breakdown.

key_findings.finding: Victoria, deaths in 2012–2013: 243 heroin-related deaths in closed coronial (NCIS) records by the authors' model, against 165 deaths with the heroin code T40.1 in AIHW national mortality data; 78 fewer in the national data. The abstract and Conclusion express this as heroin deaths 'underreported by 32%' (78 of 243); the Discussion as an actual number 47% greater than 165 (78 of 165).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results and Conclusions; Results › The number of heroin-related death cases reported, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph; Conclusion
key_findings.note: The two percentages share the numerator 78 and differ in denominator (editors' calculation: 78/243 = 32.1%, 78/165 = 47.3%). 78 is a net difference: 82 reference deaths lacked T40.1 and 4 coded deaths were excluded by the model.

key_findings.finding: Of 9,060 NCIS records returned by the search, 243 met the model's criteria: 235 heroin toxicity deaths and 8 deaths from misadventure as a result of heroin intoxication; 6-acetylmorphine was detected in 180.
key_findings.locator: Results › The number of heroin-related death cases reported, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: So 63 reference deaths (26%) rested on the morphine-to-codeine ratio or morphine alone with investigative evidence (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: All 165 AIHW heroin deaths were among the NCIS search results. Of the 243 reference deaths, 161 had T40.1; 4 more deaths with T40.1 were excluded because the model judged heroin use coincidental rather than a direct contributor; 82 reference deaths had no T40.1 and so were not counted as heroin-related in the AIHW and ABS data.
key_findings.locator: Results › The number of heroin-related death cases reported, 2nd paragraph; Results › Discrepancies in the assigned classification and coding › Comparison of the cases assigned the heroin-specific ICD-10 code of T40.1

key_findings.finding: By ICD-10 underlying-cause code, AIHW against reference counts: X42 (accidental poisoning by narcotics and psychodysleptics) 75 against 79; X44 (accidental poisoning by other and unspecified drugs) 69 against 98, the largest difference (29); Y14 10 against 12; Y12 4 against 5; F11 1 against 3; X64 6 against 6; X62 0 against 0; another underlying code, 20 reference deaths; no code at all, 20 reference deaths.
key_findings.locator: Results › Variation in the underlying Cause of Death ICD-10 coding, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1
key_findings.note: The AIHW column includes the 4 deaths the model excluded, so row differences are net; the text calls the X44 difference 29 missed cases.

key_findings.finding: 20 reference deaths had no ICD-10 code for either the underlying or the associated cause. Time from death to case closure for them: median 15.5 months (IQR 6 months), range 10 to 30 months. The authors conclude closure time was not the cause and judge it most reasonable that the deaths were reported late at initial registration and so never assessed for coding by the ABS.
key_findings.locator: Results › Variation in the underlying Cause of Death ICD-10 coding, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: No registration dates and no closure times for coded deaths are reported; the explanation is reached by elimination.

key_findings.finding: Reference deaths by how the coroner's finding attributed the death (heroin named in the certified cause of death or in the NCIS object field), with the number coded T40.1: heroin toxicity 146 of 180 (81%); heroin and morphine toxicity 8 of 11 (73%); morphine or another opioid 5 of 39 (13%); generic drug toxicity naming neither 0 of 5 (0%); misadventure from heroin intoxication 2 of 8 (25%); total 161 of 243 (66%).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Identified causes of variation in the classification and coding, definition of attribution; Results › Variation in heroin attribution or cause of death certification, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Of 191 deaths the coroner attributed to heroin, alone or with other drugs, 154 (81%) were coded T40.1 and 37 were not. In 3 of the 37 heroin was stated in the cause of death but only the generic opioid code T40.2 was assigned. Most of the rest were missed because of how the cause was worded: generic terms such as mixed or combined drug toxicity, with the contributing drugs listed only in the NCIS object field; morphine in the cause-of-death field with heroin listed only as the object; or a complication such as hypoxic brain injury listed first, in the setting of heroin use or toxicity.
key_findings.locator: Results › Variation in heroin attribution or cause of death certification, 1st and 2nd paragraphs and the list that follows
key_findings.note: The number of deaths of each kind is not reported. The 20 deaths with no code at all (late registration, key finding 4) are not broken down by attribution group, so some of the 37 may never have been coded rather than missed through wording; the paper's 'vast majority' through wording is the authors' judgement, not shown in numbers. If the abstract's 30% (about 25 of 82) refers to these deaths, roughly a dozen of the 37 would be late registrations (editors' inference).

key_findings.finding: Of 44 drug-toxicity deaths not attributed to heroin in the certification (39 morphine or another opioid, 5 generic drug toxicity), 5 (11%) were nevertheless coded T40.1.
key_findings.locator: Results › Variation in heroin attribution or cause of death certification, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: The abstract's breakdown of missed deaths: 40% from attribution to morphine toxicity or non-specific drug-toxicity certification; 30% attributed to heroin but with irregular certification; 24% from late initial registration with the Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, after which the ABS did not assess them for coding. The Discussion repeats the 40% and 30%.
key_findings.note: Not reproducible from the tables (reporting issue 1): Table 2 puts 39, 37 and 6 of the 82 missed deaths in these groups (48%, 45% and 7%), and the 20 uncoded deaths (24% of 82) cut across them (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: The only published secondary report found for the period that used ABS data and covered Victoria (Australia's Annual Overdose Report 2016) gave 220 heroin-related deaths nationally for 2012 and 2013.
key_findings.locator: Results › The number of heroin-related death cases reported, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Why heroin may be missed, as the authors describe from the literature: heroin is rapidly converted to 6-acetylmorphine and then to morphine, so morphine found after death may come from heroin or from morphine itself; after a long interval between use and death, including resuscitation and hospital admission, 6-acetylmorphine may not be detected; 6-acetylmorphine redistributes after death and is unstable in stored samples, including frozen ones; multiple drug use is common.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Heroin-related deaths and study period, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: How the counts are produced in Australia: reportable deaths go to the coroner and are first registered with the state Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, which informs the ABS; after the coroner's formal finding the certified cause reaches the NCIS; ABS mortality coders assign ICD-10 codes from both sources; the ABS reports to the AIHW. ABS data are preliminary when first published, revised the next year and final after the second year; cases still open at first coding are revised as the NCIS receives information.

The authors' stated limitation: since 2012–2013 the ABS revision process has changed; before, only the underlying cause was revised, while associated-cause toxicity codes are now also revised when more information becomes available.

The two counts were not defined alike. The national comparison count took deaths with T40.1 as an associated cause only when the underlying cause was a drug poisoning (X42, X44, X62, X64, X85, Y12, Y14) or, before 2013, F11 or F19, while the reference also included 8 deaths from misadventure as a result of heroin intoxication. Of the 82 reference deaths without T40.1, 20 had another underlying-cause code, outside the national definition, and 20 had no ICD-10 code at all; the other 42 had a poisoning or F11 underlying cause (editors' calculation from Table 1: 203 reference deaths in those rows, 161 of them coded T40.1). How the 8 misadventure deaths and the 20 uncoded deaths are distributed across these groups and the attribution groups of Table 2 is not cross-tabulated.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Heroin-related deaths from the AIHW and ABS, bullet list (p. 7); Results › The number of heroin-related death cases reported, 1st paragraph (p. 9); Results › Variation in the underlying Cause of Death ICD-10 coding, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 10); Table 1 (p. 19)
key_findings.note: Part of the 78-death net shortfall therefore reflects the difference in definitions and late registration, not miscoding of deaths the national count was designed to capture (editors' reading).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's shares of missed deaths (40% attributed to morphine or certified as non-specific drug toxicity; 30% attributed to heroin with irregular certification; 24% late registration) state no denominator and cannot be reproduced from Tables 1 and 2. Of the 82 reference deaths without T40.1, Table 2 places 39 in the morphine, other-opioid or generic groups, 37 in the heroin-attributed groups and 6 among misadventure deaths, while the 20 uncoded deaths (20 of 82 = 24%) are not assigned to these groups.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 40% and 30% would fit 82 missed deaths only if the 20 uncoded deaths were first removed from the attribution groups (about 33 and 25 deaths; editors' calculation), which the paper does not show. Claims should cite the table counts, not the abstract's shares.

reporting_issues.issue: The shortfall is given three ways: 78 fewer deaths (net), heroin deaths 'underreported by 32%' (78 of 243) and an actual number 47% greater than 165 (78 of 165); meanwhile 82 reference deaths lacked T40.1 and 4 coded deaths were excluded by the model. The per-code differences in Table 1 (e.g., 29 for X44) are also net, because the AIHW column contains the 4 excluded deaths.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should say which figure they use: the heroin code was missing from 82 of 243 reference deaths (34%); the national count was 78 (32%) lower than the reference count; 4 coded deaths were judged not heroin-related.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say two (25%) of the eight misadventure deaths were specifically attributed to heroin in the cause-of-death certification, whereas Table 2's figure for that row, 2 (25%), is the number assigned T40.1.
reporting_issues.consequence: How many misadventure deaths named heroin on the certificate is unclear; 2 of 8 is certain only as the number coded T40.1.

reporting_issues.issue: The same number, 180, is given for deaths in which 6-acetylmorphine was detected (Results, 1st paragraph) and for deaths attributed to heroin toxicity alone (Results; Table 2); attribution is not cross-tabulated by 6-acetylmorphine detection.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether coroners' attribution to heroin followed 6-acetylmorphine detection, and how many deaths in each attribution group rest on weaker markers, cannot be determined.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results give 220 heroin-related deaths nationally for 2012–2013 from Australia's Annual Overdose Report 2016, and the Discussion calls this a demonstration of variability in a secondary report, without explaining how the figure was derived or how it relates to Victoria's 165 (AIHW) and 243 (reference) deaths.
reporting_issues.consequence: The national figure is lower than Victoria's own reference count; the paper does not establish why, so it should not be cited as a measure of national underreporting.

reporting_issues.issue: The accepted manuscript's conflict-of-interest declaration reads that no other authors declare a conflict, but no declaration for any author precedes it.
reporting_issues.consequence: A declared interest may be missing from this version; the version of record should be checked before the funding field is finalized.

Darke's commentary (doi 10.1111/add.14520) and Robertson's letter (doi 10.1111/add.14627) were not among the files and were not read.
